sentences.text: Unlike later tyrannosaurs, Guanlong possessed three long fingers on its hands and likely resembled its close relative Dilong with a coat of primitive feathers.
The animal featured a highly pneumatized cranial crest similar to those of Dilophosaurus and Monolophosaurus, which likely served as display organs for mating events.
Fossil evidence shows one specimen found lying on top of another along with three other theropod dinosaurs.
A juvenile individual died at six years of age while still growing.

Guanlong was first described in 2006 by Xu Xing and colleagues as a new taxon related to Tyrannosaurus, discovered in the Dzungaria area of China by a joint expedition between the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology and George Washington University.
Researchers presume the immature specimen was trampled to death by the adult individual after both died.
Juvenile Guanlong exhibited features such as a proportionally shorter snout, larger orbits, larger hands, longer lower legs, and a less expanded pubic bone compared to adults.

A 2013 study classified Guanlong in the family Proceratosauridae alongside Proceratosaurus and Kileskus, while a 2014 study redefined the family to include only Guanlong, Proceratosaurus, Kileskus, and Sinotyrannus.
A 2024 study placed Dilong and proceratosaurids like Guanlong outside the clade Tyrannosauroidea based on phylogenetic analysis.
Guanlong lived about 160 million years ago during the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic, with estimates ranging between 161.5 and 154.8 million years ago.
While crests in related genera may have been for species recognition, the gracile crest of Guanlong is more likely used for display purposes.
